title: Her style on tenor, flute and baritone
summary: She is not a bebopper; Royal Stokes called her a keeper of the flame, with Lester Young, Hawkins and Lucky Thompson on tenor, Latin on flute, lyrical baritone; they admire Nick Brignola and Pepper Adams.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Did you have a particular style of jazz that you pursued? Were you going to be a bebopper? Or is that too simplistic?

I wish I were a bebopper. I really don’t have the language, you know, the way some people do. There might be hints of it in my playing. But my — in one book, Royal Stokes’ book, he put me in the chapter “keepers of the flame.” I guess that a lot of people find elements of Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins in my playing on tenor. And my, well one of my super favorites is Lucky Thompson. So, even though they’re all so great, all the tenor players.
Yes. You can get something from just about everybody, right?

Yeah. And then on flute I kind of always drifted a lot towards the Latin, that percussive, pungent sort of style. But I love playing obbligatos too, and ballads, and almost any era I guess. I liked to play the really really old tunes too, 30s tunes in a humorous way. And then on baritone I mean I leaned toward seeing it as a very lyrical, melodic instrument, rather than a punching out those — I like doing those too — honking out the notes. But for some reason I just find it a very —
Or the, was it Nick Brignola, who like he could play bop on the baritone like he was playing an alto.
Just like it was nothing, yeah, Nick and Pepper, oh my God they just — so marvelous, I would love to — but that’s not within my reach. It’s just something I can’t do.
